explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. The psalm says Israel left "…a people of foreign tongue…" (Psalm 114:1). In plain words, the people in Egypt spoke a language that wasn't theirs. Picture moving to a place where nobody understands a word you say, and you just point at things for years.

Here's what the text says: Israel departed from "…a people of foreign tongue…" (Psalm 114:1). A foreign tongue means a language that wasn't Israel's own. So the people in Egypt did speak differently from them. Easy one to flip, friend, like a cookie that looks done but isn't.

Yes, friend. The psalm says "Judah became God’s sanctuary…" (Psalm 114:2). A sanctuary is a holy place set apart for God. When Israel left Egypt, Judah became His special place. That's a BIG promotion.

A footstool shows up in other places in the Bible (Isaiah 66:1), but not here. Psalm 114:2 says "Judah became God’s sanctuary…" A sanctuary is a holy place set apart for God. I'd say a footstool is where you put your feet, and this is a whole different kind of honor.

Close to the neighborhood, but not the address. The psalm says "Judah became God’s sanctuary…" (Psalm 114:2). A vineyard is a place for growing grapes, and this verse isn't talking about one. A sanctuary is a holy place set apart for God.

You got it, baker. The psalm says "The sea observed and fled…" (Psalm 114:3). It saw what was happening and took off. I think that's the fastest exit anybody has ever made, and I once left a junk drawer.
The text says the opposite. "The sea observed and fled…" (Psalm 114:3). It didn't stand its ground or stay put. It saw what was happening and ran, no goodbyes.

That's it, baker. The psalm says, "the Jordan turned back…" (Psalm 114:3). First the sea fled, and then the Jordan turned back. A river turning back is like a conveyor belt running backward. You blink twice and check the label.
Red is a good guess, but the psalm doesn't mention any color. It says "the Jordan turned back…" (Psalm 114:3). The Jordan turned around, and that's the whole line. Nothing in it is about color.

A wild river sounds exciting, but that's not what the psalm says. It says "the Jordan turned back…" (Psalm 114:3). The Jordan is a river, and it reversed course. It's the calmest kind of wild, if you ask me.

The picture isn't crumbling, friend. The psalm says "…the mountains skipped like rams, the hills like lambs." (Psalm 114:4). Skipping is lively movement, like young animals bouncing around. Nothing in the verse says they fell apart.

Right, it's false. The psalm says "…the mountains skipped like rams, the hills like lambs." (Psalm 114:4). Rams and lambs skip and bounce, so the picture is lively motion. Crumbling away isn't in the verse. Mountains with that much bounce, and I can't even get my hat to sit straight.

Exactly. The psalmist asks, "Why was it, O sea, that you fled, O Jordan, that you turned back…" (Psalm 114:5). Then the mountains and hills get asked why they skipped (Psalm 114:6). The question is why they moved.

Good thinking, but that's not the question. He asks, "Why was it, O sea, that you fled, O Jordan, that you turned back…" (Psalm 114:5). He asks the mountains and hills why they skipped (Psalm 114:6). He wants to know why they moved, not where they were headed.

Nothing in the psalm asks about coming back. He asks, "Why was it, O sea, that you fled, O Jordan, that you turned back…" (Psalm 114:5). Then the mountains and hills get asked why they skipped (Psalm 114:6). It's all about why they moved.

Yes, friend. The psalm says, "Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord…" (Psalm 114:7). The whole earth is told to shake in the presence of the God of Jacob. Even my knees get wobbly when the oven timer goes off, and that's just a timer.

Rising is a fair guess for a big moment. But the psalm says, "Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord…" (Psalm 114:7). The earth is told to tremble, to shake, in His presence. It isn't told to stand up.

Rest sounds peaceful, friend, but this verse isn't a lullaby. It says, "Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord…" (Psalm 114:7). The earth is told to tremble before the God of Jacob. No napping on this one.
That's the one. The psalm says God "…turned the rock into a pool…" (Psalm 114:8). A hard rock became a pool of water. That's like hitting a dead end and finding a swimming pool waiting there.

A tower is a natural thing to build from a rock, but that's not what happened here. The psalm says God "…turned the rock into a pool…" (Psalm 114:8). A hard rock became a pool of water. Towers go up, and this one gave water.

An altar can be made of stones, as in Exodus 20:25, but not in this verse. The psalm says God "…turned the rock into a pool…" (Psalm 114:8). The rock became water, and the flint became "…a fountain of water!" in the same verse.

That's the picture, friend. The sea fled, the Jordan turned back, the mountains skipped, and the earth is told to tremble before "…the God of Jacob…" (Psalm 114:7). Even a rock turned into a pool (Psalm 114:8). Nothing in this psalm is outside His reach.

Judah became His sanctuary (Psalm 114:2), but the psalm doesn't stop there. The sea fled, the Jordan turned back, the mountains and hills skipped (Psalm 114:3-4), and the earth is told to tremble before Him (Psalm 114:7). His power reaches far past Judah.

explanations.answer: He stays far from His people
explanations.explanation: The psalm says the opposite. Judah became "…God’s sanctuary, Israel His dominion." (Psalm 114:2). He's close to His people, and the earth is told to tremble at "…the presence of the God of Jacob…" (Psalm 114:7). That's not a far-off God.
